meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If the American people ever allow private banks to control the issue of their currency, first by inflation, then by deflation, the banks and corporations that will grow up around them will deprive the people of all property until their children wake up homeless on the continent their fathers conquered'?
meta.ogDescription: A famous banking warning pinned on Thomas Jefferson. Monticello finds it in none of his writings; “inflation” and “deflation” postdate him. First seen in print in 1933.

answer.label: Not Thomas Jefferson — a 20th-century fabrication
answer.authorDates: 1743–1826 · 3rd U.S. President; principal author of the Declaration of Independence
answer.sourceLine: Jefferson was a genuine critic of banks, but this exact passage is spurious. The Thomas Jefferson Foundation reports it appears in none of his writings, and its very vocabulary betrays it: the words “inflation” and “deflation” are not documented in this monetary sense until after his lifetime. It surfaces in print only in 1933 — over a century after Jefferson died — and is often falsely tied to a non-existent 1809 pamphlet, The Debate Over the Recharter of the Bank Bill.

source.excerpt: If the American people ever allow private banks to control the issue of their currency, first by inflation, then by deflation, the banks and corporations that will grow up around them will deprive the people of all property until their children wake up homeless on the continent their Fathers conquered.
trail: The Thomas Jefferson Foundation states the “private banks…wake up homeless” passage “has not been found anywhere in Thomas Jefferson’s writings,” and notes the words “inflation” and “deflation” are not documented until after his lifetime — per Monticello’s spurious-quotation entry.
The earliest located appearance in print is 1933, when Texas Rep. Wright Patman used it — “Patman Argues for Payment in Money,” Dallas Morning News, 16 Jan 1933.

Jefferson’s genuine bank warning is milder and real: “banking establishments are more dangerous than standing armies… swindling futurity on a large scale,” from his letter to John Taylor, 28 May 1816.
Snopes and Respectfully Quoted (Library of Congress) likewise flag the passage as unverified and anachronistic.
source.excerptNote: The wording circulated by itself; it is often padded with two further lines — a misquotation of Jefferson’s genuine 1816 letter to John Taylor (“banking establishments are more dangerous than standing armies”) and a loose echo of his 1813 letter to John Wayles Eppes — to lend it a Jeffersonian ring.
source.rightsNote: The exact viral wording is an unsourced fabrication of unknown authorship, first documented in 1933 and traceable to no Jefferson text or any identifiable original writer — so no copyright or public-domain status can be responsibly asserted. Jefferson’s own writings (e.g. the 1816 Taylor letter) are long in the public domain, but that does not cover this concocted passage.

author.name: Thomas Jefferson
author.heading: About Thomas Jefferson
author.metaLine: 1743–1826 · 3rd U.S. President & principal author of the Declaration of Independence
author.bio: Thomas Jefferson (1743–1826) was the principal author of the Declaration of Independence and the third President of the United States. He was a genuine and outspoken critic of banks, paper money, and public debt — which is exactly why fabricated warnings about “private banks” attach so easily to his name. His authentic bank writings, such as the 1816 letter to John Taylor, are pointed but never used the modern words “inflation” and “deflation” found in the viral passage.

misattribution.heading: How a fabrication got Jefferson’s name
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-circulated fake Jefferson quotations on the internet — a hard-money warning stitched together and antedated by more than a century.

items.why: The Thomas Jefferson Foundation reports the passage “has not been found anywhere in Thomas Jefferson’s writings, to Albert Gallatin or otherwise,” and that the monetary terms “inflation” and “deflation” postdate his life — per Monticello.
Monticello finds “no record of any publication called The Debate Over the Recharter of the Bank Bill,” and the wording appears in no 1802 Gallatin correspondence — Monticello.

items.scope: The appended “more dangerous than standing armies” line
items.why: This tag-along sentence is Jefferson — a slight misquotation of his 28 May 1816 letter to John Taylor — which lends the fabricated portion false credibility.

misattribution.truthLine: Jefferson distrusted banks, but he never wrote this: the “wake up homeless” passage is absent from his works, uses words that entered the language after he died, and first appears in print in 1933 — see Monticello’s entry.

context.heading: Why the fake persists
lead: The passage thrives because it fuses a real Jeffersonian sentiment — deep suspicion of concentrated financial power — with vivid, modern economic imagery he never used. Jefferson genuinely warned that “banking establishments are more dangerous than standing armies” in an 1816 letter to John Taylor, so the forgery feels plausible to anyone who knows his politics.

Its modern career began in monetary-reform and hard-money circles: it was quoted by Rep. Wright Patman in 1933 and has since been a fixture of anti-central-bank and gold-standard rhetoric, spreading through chain emails and social media where a famous name matters more than a footnote.
detailsBody: Authentic: “And I sincerely believe with you, that banking establishments are more dangerous than standing armies; & that the principle of spending money to be paid by posterity, under the name of funding, is but swindling futurity on a large scale.” — to John Taylor, 28 May 1816.

Authentic: “Bank-paper must be suppressed, and the circulating medium must be restored to the nation to whom it belongs.” — to John Wayles Eppes, 1813, the likely raw material for the fabricated “issuing power” line.
context.pull: A real sentiment, in words Jefferson never had — ‘inflation’ and ‘deflation’ entered the language after he died.
